content: Health insurance has the potential to enhance access to healthcare services and shield individuals from the financial burdens associated with illnesses. However, coverage rates are often insufficient, particularly among those who are most vulnerable, such as children and other at-risk groups. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various strategies aimed at increasing health insurance coverage among vulnerable populations. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, Global Health, and others, up until November 2012. Additional searches were performed in reference lists of included studies and through citation tracking using Web of Science to identify other relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (NRCTs), controlled before-and-after (CBA) studies, and interrupted time series (ITS) studies. These studies needed to assess the impact of strategies designed to improve the enrollment of vulnerable populations into health insurance programs. Two broad categories and six specific strategies were identified as interventions for this purpose. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently conducted by at least two reviewers. A structured synthesis of the findings was performed. Two studies, both conducted in the United States, were included in the review. The first study demonstrated that providing health insurance information and application assistance through community-based case managers likely increased the likelihood of parents enrolling their children in health insurance programs (risk ratio [RR] 1.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.44 to 1.96, moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, these parents were more likely to maintain their children’s insurance coverage over time (RR 2.59, 95% CI 1.95 to 3.44, moderate-quality evidence). Among children who were insured, those in the intervention group may have been insured more quickly, with an average reduction of 47.3 days in the time to insurance coverage (95% CI 20.6 to 74.0 days, low-quality evidence). Parents in the intervention group also reported higher satisfaction levels on average (satisfaction score difference 1.07, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.42, low-quality evidence). The second study evaluated the impact of distributing health insurance application materials in hospital emergency departments. Compared to not distributing these materials, this intervention may have increased enrollment rates (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.18, low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that community-based case managers who provide health insurance information, assist with applications, and liaise with insurers likely improve the enrollment of children in health insurance programs. However, the generalizability of this approach to other populations or settings remains uncertain. Additionally, distributing insurance application materials in hospital emergency departments may have a positive effect on enrollment rates, though the evidence is of low quality. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of various strategies for expanding health insurance coverage in vulnerable populations, particularly in diverse settings and with rigorous study designs.
